abstract: Purpose: High-density surface electromyography (HDsEMG) quantifies the spatial distribution of muscle activity, and greater redistribution during sustained muscle contractions has been associated with longer endurance time. However, it remains unclear whether providing real-time biofeedback on the spatial distribution of muscle activity can enhance endurance. This study determined whether real-time augmented reality (AR) biofeedback on the spatial distribution of knee extensor muscle activity allowed individuals to alter the spatial activation of their muscles during dynamic contractions and improved knee extensor endurance. Methods: Fourteen healthy adults performed isokinetic knee extensions at 35% of maximal voluntary contraction torque until volitional exhaustion under two randomized conditions: with and without AR HDsEMG biofeedback. HDsEMG was recorded from the vastus lateralis and rectus femoris using a 64-electrode grid. Results: Participants completed more repetitions with biofeedback than without (p < 0.001, d = 1.41). With biofeedback, a lateral shift in the spatial distribution of muscle activity was observed (medio-lateral centroid; p = 0.022), indicating greater contribution from the lateral region of the quadriceps. Global markers of myoelectric manifestations of fatigue showed similar temporal changes in both conditions. Exploratory analyses showed no association between condition-related changes in HDsEMG variables and the individual endurance gain (all p > 0.05). Conclusions: AR biofeedback based on HDsEMG can improve muscular endurance while enabling individuals to modify spatial activation of their knee extensors during dynamic fatiguing exercise. These findings support the use of AR HDsEMG biofeedback as a novel tool to optimize neuromuscular function and potentially push the boundaries of athletic performance.
